The text examines electric-magnetic duality transformations in four-dimensional gravity, focusing on theories linearized around either Minkowski space or (anti-)de Sitter backgrounds, \((A)dS_4\). In this setting, duality transformations relate different descriptions of the same bulk gravitational degrees of freedom, in a manner analogous to electric-magnetic duality in gauge theory.

A key point is that the presence of a cosmological constant changes the role of these transformations. In flat space, electric-magnetic duality can often be implemented as a symmetry of the Hamiltonian formulation. However, when the theory is expanded around an \((A)dS_4\) background, the cosmological constant generally causes the duality transformation to alter the Hamiltonian. This means that the transformed Hamiltonian may differ from the original one, even though the transformation still maps the theory into an equivalent description.

Importantly, this modification of the Hamiltonian does not change the physical bulk dynamics. The equations of motion in the interior of spacetime remain invariant under the duality transformation, so the propagating gravitational degrees of freedom are unaffected. In this sense, the transformation preserves the local dynamics of linearized gravity, even if it changes the canonical form of the theory.

The discussion therefore pays particular attention to the boundary terms produced by these duality transformations. Since the bulk theory remains dynamically equivalent, the main nontrivial effects arise at the boundary. These boundary contributions can encode important information about how the duality acts on conserved charges, variational principles, and possible boundary degrees of freedom.

Finally, the text explores the significance of these boundary terms from the perspective of holography. In holographic settings, especially for asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes, boundary terms in the gravitational action are closely related to data in the dual field theory. The boundary contributions generated by electric-magnetic duality may therefore have a natural interpretation as transformations of the holographic stress tensor, boundary sources, or response functions. Thus, while the duality leaves the bulk gravitational dynamics unchanged, it can have meaningful consequences for the boundary theory and for the holographic dictionary.

The text studies electric-magnetic duality transformations in four-dimensional gravity, with particular attention to the theory linearized around either flat Minkowski space or constant-curvature \((A)dS_4\) backgrounds. In analogy with the familiar duality of Maxwell theory, the analysis asks how the gravitational “electric” and “magnetic” components can be exchanged, how this exchange is realized at the level of the linearized gravitational variables, and what changes it induces in the canonical formulation of the theory.

A central issue is the implementation of duality in the Hamiltonian description. For linearized gravity around Minkowski space, electric-magnetic duality can be formulated as a canonical transformation acting on the appropriate phase-space variables. In this case, the transformation preserves the bulk Hamiltonian structure, so the equations of motion and the propagating degrees of freedom are left unchanged. The duality therefore appears as a genuine symmetry of the linearized bulk dynamics.

The situation becomes subtler when the background is \((A)dS_4\), where the cosmological constant introduces additional terms into the Hamiltonian. These terms generally transform nontrivially under electric-magnetic duality. As a result, the Hamiltonian itself is not strictly invariant: the duality transformation modifies it by terms that are sensitive to the curvature scale of the background. Nevertheless, this modification does not alter the local bulk equations of motion. The physical bulk dynamics remains equivalent before and after the duality transformation, showing that the cosmological constant obstructs invariance of the Hamiltonian in form, but not the equivalence of the underlying linearized dynamics.

The analysis also emphasizes the role of boundary terms. Under duality transformations, changes in the Hamiltonian or action can often be expressed as total derivatives or surface contributions. These boundary terms are not merely technical artifacts; in gravitational theories, especially in asymptotically anti-de Sitter spaces, they are physically meaningful. They affect the definition of conserved charges, the variational principle, and the relation between bulk gravitational fields and boundary data.

This has important implications for holography. In the AdS/CFT correspondence, bulk gravitational dynamics is encoded in a dual conformal field theory living at the boundary. Therefore, a transformation that leaves the bulk equations unchanged but modifies boundary terms may correspond to a nontrivial transformation of the boundary theory. Electric-magnetic duality in the gravitational bulk can thus be interpreted as inducing a change in boundary variables, boundary conditions, or correlation functions. In particular, the duality may relate different holographic descriptions that share the same bulk propagating content but differ in their boundary interpretation.

Overall, the text shows that gravitational electric-magnetic duality is a robust feature of linearized four-dimensional gravity, but its precise realization depends on the background geometry. In flat space, it behaves as a symmetry of the Hamiltonian formulation, while in the presence of a cosmological constant it changes the Hamiltonian by boundary-related contributions without modifying the bulk dynamics. The resulting boundary terms are essential for understanding the full physical meaning of the duality, especially in holographic settings where boundary data carry the observable content of the theory.
outputs.L5:
Minkowski space and Hamiltonian mechanics are two important concepts in theoretical physics, especially in relativity and field theory.

Minkowski space is the mathematical setting of special relativity. It combines three dimensions of space with one dimension of time into a four-dimensional spacetime. Unlike ordinary Euclidean space, Minkowski space has a metric with a different sign for the time component, which allows it to describe the invariant spacetime interval between events. This structure makes it possible to analyze motion, causality, and the behavior of light in a relativistically consistent way.

The Hamiltonian, on the other hand, is a central concept in classical and quantum mechanics. In classical mechanics, the Hamiltonian is usually interpreted as the total energy of a system, expressed in terms of positions and momenta. It generates the time evolution of the system through Hamilton’s equations. In quantum mechanics, the Hamiltonian becomes an operator that determines how the state of a system changes over time.

The connection between Minkowski space and the Hamiltonian becomes especially important in relativistic physics. In a relativistic theory, energy and momentum are combined into a four-vector, and the Hamiltonian is associated with the energy component of this vector. For a free relativistic particle in Minkowski space, the energy satisfies the relation

\[
E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4,
\]

where \(E\) is energy, \(p\) is momentum, \(m\) is mass, and \(c\) is the speed of light. In this context, the Hamiltonian can be written as

\[
H = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}.
\]

This expression shows how the Hamiltonian must be modified when the geometry of spacetime is Minkowskian rather than purely Newtonian.

In field theory, the Hamiltonian describes the energy of fields defined over Minkowski spacetime. It plays a key role in determining the dynamics of classical fields and in constructing quantum field theories. While the Lagrangian formulation often makes Lorentz symmetry more explicit, the Hamiltonian formulation is essential for studying time evolution, quantization, and conserved quantities.

Thus, Minkowski space provides the geometric framework for relativistic physics, while the Hamiltonian provides a powerful way to describe the dynamics of particles and fields within that framework. Together, they form a foundation for modern theories of matter, energy, and spacetime.

counterfactuals.output: We study electric-magnetic duality for linearized gravity in four dimensions on Minkowski and constant-curvature \((A)dS\) backgrounds. Using the gauge-invariant decomposition of the spin-2 field, we formulate the duality as an interchange between the electric and magnetic components of the linearized Weyl tensor, and show how the equations of motion and Bianchi identities are exchanged. Particular attention is paid to the role of boundary terms in the quadratic gravitational action: while they do not affect the local bulk dynamics, they are essential for a well-defined variational principle, for the action of duality on canonical variables, and for identifying conserved charges. In asymptotically AdS settings, these boundary contributions naturally connect the bulk duality rotation to transformations of the boundary stress tensor and Cotton tensor, suggesting a holographic interpretation as a gravitational analogue of electric-magnetic duality in the dual conformal field theory. We also comment on the modifications introduced by the cosmological constant and on the relation between flat-space and \((A)dS\) dual formulations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study of how duality transformations act in 4D linearized gravity with a cosmological constant, emphasizing effects on the Hamiltonian and boundary contributions.
counterfactuals.output:
The study examines electric–magnetic–type duality in four-dimensional linearized gravity when the background is not flat but has a cosmological constant, i.e. linear perturbations around de Sitter or anti–de Sitter space.

Its main conclusions can be summarized as follows:

- **Duality still acts on the physical spin-2 degrees of freedom.**  
  After performing a Hamiltonian/ADM decomposition and solving the linearized constraints, the two propagating graviton polarizations can be written in terms of dual variables or “prepotentials.” A duality rotation exchanges these variables in a way analogous to electric–magnetic rotations in Maxwell theory.

- **The bulk equations remain compatible with duality.**  
  The linearized Einstein equations with cosmological constant can be reorganized so that the duality transformation rotates the “electric” and “magnetic” parts of the linearized Weyl tensor. Thus, at the level of local field equations, the presence of Λ does not destroy the duality structure.

- **The Hamiltonian is more subtle.**  
  In flat space, the duality transformation leaves the Hamiltonian invariant up to harmless total derivatives. With a cosmological constant, the Hamiltonian contains additional Λ-dependent pieces coming from the curved background. These terms are not individually invariant under the duality rotation, but their variation can be reorganized into boundary contributions.

- **Boundary terms become essential.**  
  The transformation of the Hamiltonian is not simply zero; it differs by surface terms. If one imposes boundary conditions under which these surface integrals vanish, then duality is a symmetry of the bulk Hamiltonian theory. But for more general boundary conditions—especially in asymptotically AdS or dS settings—the surface terms can carry physical information.

- **Duality rotates boundary data and charges.**  
  The boundary contributions are related to gravitational charges, such as mass-like and NUT-like quantities, or more generally the electric and magnetic components of the asymptotic Weyl tensor. Duality therefore does not merely act on local propagating modes; it also mixes boundary charges.

- **The cosmological constant does not eliminate duality, but it changes its canonical realization.**  
  The key result is that duality remains a meaningful symmetry of the linearized bulk theory, yet its action on the Hamiltonian is only well defined once boundary terms and boundary conditions are carefully specified.

In short: the study shows that 4D linearized gravity with a cosmological constant still admits a gravitational electric–magnetic duality, but the Hamiltonian is invariant only up to boundary terms. Those boundary terms are not merely technical artifacts; in spacetimes with nontrivial asymptotic structure they encode physical charges and determine whether the duality is an exact symmetry of the full canonical theory.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: Electric–magnetic duality in gravity can be implemented at the linearized level by exploiting the curvature, rather than the metric perturbation, as the fundamental gauge-invariant object. Around flat spacetime, the linearized Riemann tensor admits a dualization on one pair of antisymmetric indices, and the linearized Einstein equations and Bianchi identities are interchanged in close analogy with Maxwell theory. This permits the introduction of a dual graviton potential whose Curvature encodes the dual Riemann tensor, though its formulation is generally non-local or requires mixed-symmetry fields and additional gauge redundancies. In anti-de Sitter or de Sitter backgrounds, the construction is modified by the nonzero cosmological constant: the relevant field strengths are built from covariantized linearized curvatures, and duality must respect the background isometry group and the altered relation between Bianchi identities and equations of motion. While fully covariant, local actions realizing gravitational duality remain difficult to construct, especially beyond the free theory, the linearized framework provides a precise setting in which dual descriptions of spin-2 dynamics and their dependence on spacetime curvature can be systematically analyzed.

counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract:**  
We investigate electric–magnetic duality in linearized gravity, focusing on its consequences for bulk dynamics, Hamiltonian formulations, and holographic boundary structures. Starting from the Pauli–Fierz description of a massless spin-2 field, we reformulate the theory in terms of dual variables and analyze the symmetry that exchanges the linearized Riemann tensor with its Hodge dual. We show that, while the bulk equations of motion admit a duality-covariant interpretation analogous to Maxwell theory, the realization of this symmetry at the level of the action and Hamiltonian requires a careful treatment of constraints, gauge redundancies, and boundary contributions. In the canonical formalism, the Hamiltonian can be expressed in terms of electric and magnetic components of the linearized Weyl tensor, making the duality structure manifest up to total derivative terms. We further examine the role of boundary terms in asymptotically AdS and flat backgrounds, emphasizing how duality transformations act on holographic data such as the boundary stress tensor and its magnetic counterpart. The analysis reveals that gravitational electric–magnetic duality not only reorganizes the propagating bulk degrees of freedom but also induces a nontrivial map between boundary sources, responses, and conserved charges. These results clarify the extent to which linearized gravitational duality is a genuine symmetry of the full variational principle and provide a framework for understanding its implications in holography, including possible dual descriptions of boundary energy–momentum dynamics and gravitational response functions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short research summary on duality rotations in four-dimensional linearized gravity around Minkowski or (A)dS4 backgrounds and their holographic implications.
counterfactuals.output:
Duality rotations in four-dimensional linearized gravity generalize the familiar electric–magnetic duality of Maxwell theory. Around Minkowski space, the linearized Riemann/Weyl tensor can be decomposed into “electric” and “magnetic” parts with respect to a time slicing,  
\[
E_{ij}=C_{0i0j},\qquad B_{ij}=\frac12 \epsilon_i{}^{kl} C_{0jkl},
\]
which are symmetric, traceless, and transverse on shell. The vacuum linearized Einstein equations are invariant under an \(SO(2)\) rotation
\[
\begin{pmatrix}E\\ B\end{pmatrix}
\to
\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & \sin\theta\\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}E\\ B\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This symmetry is not manifest in the usual metric formulation, but it becomes explicit in Hamiltonian or “prepotential” formulations, where the two helicity-2 degrees of freedom are described by a pair of dual symmetric tensors. In this language, the constraints of linearized gravity are solved analogously to Gauss’ law in electromagnetism, and the duality rotation acts locally on the prepotentials.

The construction extends, with modifications, to maximally symmetric backgrounds such as \((A)dS_4\). The cosmological constant changes the form of the linearized equations and the constraint algebra, but the physical helicity-2 sector still admits an electric/magnetic decomposition of the Weyl tensor. In conformally flat backgrounds, including \(AdS_4\) and \(dS_4\), the Weyl tensor remains the natural gauge-invariant object, and linearized Einstein equations again imply a duality relation between its electric and magnetic components. The presence of the curvature scale introduces additional terms in canonical formulations, but the underlying exchange of the two transverse-traceless graviton polarizations survives.

The holographic significance is especially clear in \(AdS_4/CFT_3\). For asymptotically \(AdS_4\) perturbations, the boundary metric perturbation acts as the source for the three-dimensional CFT stress tensor \(T_{ij}\). The “magnetic” part of the bulk Weyl tensor is related near the boundary to the Cotton tensor \(C_{ij}\) of the boundary metric, while the “electric” part is related to the expectation value of the CFT stress tensor. Thus bulk gravitational duality rotates, schematically,
\[
T_{ij} \leftrightarrow C_{ij}.
\]
This resembles electric–magnetic duality in bulk gauge fields, where boundary currents and background gauge fields are exchanged. In the gravitational case, the operation maps ordinary boundary conditions to mixed or alternative boundary conditions and can be interpreted as a canonical transformation on the boundary phase space.

Consequently, gravitational duality in \(AdS_4\) suggests a three-dimensional “dual CFT” operation acting on the stress-tensor sector. It exchanges stress-tensor data with the Cotton tensor of the boundary geometry and is closely related to adding gravitational Chern–Simons/contact terms or performing an \(S\)-type transformation on the CFT generating functional. This provides a geometric realization of holographic duality transformations and clarifies how bulk helicity rotations are encoded in boundary conformal data.

In summary, duality rotations in four-dimensional linearized gravity reveal a hidden \(SO(2)\) symmetry of the helicity-2 equations, most transparent at the level of Weyl curvature or canonical prepotentials. Around Minkowski and \((A)dS_4\) backgrounds, they interchange electric and magnetic gravitational fields. In \(AdS_4\), this interchange acquires a holographic meaning: the bulk duality maps boundary stress-tensor expectation values to Cotton-tensor data, relating different boundary conditions and suggesting a gravitational analogue of electric–magnetic duality in the dual three-dimensional CFT.
